analysis.one_liner: Caps jury awards for pain and suffering in medical malpractice cases at $250,000 and shields drugmakers who follow FDA rules.
analysis.headline: Despite 141 cosponsors, the bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overridden state medical malpractice laws nationwide. It capped compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and lost companionship at $250,000 no matter how severe the injury, made punitive damages nearly impossible to win, and barred punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products were approved by the FDA. It also capped lawyers' contingency fees and shortened the window for filing claims. Supporters argued this would lower doctors' malpractice insurance costs and health care prices; opponents said it would cap what the most grievously injured patients could recover.
analysis.who_benefits: Malpractice insurers, whose payouts would be capped and more predictable; doctors, hospitals, and nursing homes facing suits; and drug and device manufacturers, who would gain near-immunity from punitive damages for FDA-approved products. Patients who win suits would keep more of the award after the attorney-fee caps and would be protected against insurers taking liens on their recoveries.

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic damages at $250,000 while leaving economic damages (medical bills, lost earnings) unlimited, reducing defendants' exposure to large jury awards [S2][S3].

Bars punitive damages against drug, device, and biologics manufacturers for products approved or cleared by the FDA, unless the company withheld required information from the FDA or bribed an FDA official [S2][S3].

Caps plaintiffs' contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% above $600,000) and lets courts supervise fee arrangements, leaving more of any recovery with the claimant [S2][S3].

Prohibits providers of collateral source benefits (health insurers, government programs) from recovering liens or credits against a patient's award, and allows proportional rather than joint liability so each defendant pays only its own share [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients seriously injured by medical negligence. The $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages falls hardest on people with small economic losses — children, retirees, and stay-at-home caregivers — because the cap binds exactly when lost wages and medical bills are low but the injury is catastrophic. States would lose the power to set their own rules for malpractice cases.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages applies regardless of how many defendants or claims are involved, so a child or retired person left severely disabled by negligence — someone with little lost income — could recover at most $250,000 for a lifetime of pain and lost enjoyment of life [S2][S3].

Punitive damages would require clear and convincing proof of deliberate intent to injure, a bar almost no negligence or recklessness case can meet, and juries would not even be told the cap exists [S2][S3].

The FDA-compliance shield would block punitive damages even where later evidence shows a drug or device was dangerous, and the bill preempts state laws that give injured patients stronger remedies, overriding state courts and legislatures [S3].

Supporters' central claim — that these caps would lower malpractice premiums and health care costs — was contested, and the bill contained no mechanism guaranteeing that insurers' savings would be passed to patients or doctors [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have helped doctors and insurers predictably by capping their worst-case liability, and it did include some patient-side features (unlimited economic damages, fee caps, limits on insurer liens). But its main effect was to take money from the most catastrophically injured patients — those with the least provable lost income — and shield pharmaceutical manufacturers from punitive damages, while overriding state laws chosen by state legislatures and juries. Whether savings would reach patients through lower premiums was asserted, not guaranteed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees and sent to the Judiciary Committee's Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote for the rest of the Congress [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Cox introduced the bill on February 2, 2005, with 141 cosponsors — 136 Republicans and 5 Democrats [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees, and on February 25, 2005, to the Judiciary Committee's Health Subcommittee [S5].

No further action appears in the record for the rest of the 109th Congress; the bill never received a subcommittee markup, a committee vote, or a House floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Malpractice insurers, hospitals, and drugmakers who would have gained capped liability keep the existing, more open-ended liability system, as do plaintiffs' trial lawyers whose contingency fees would have been capped. Injured patients also keep whatever their state law currently allows, since no federal cap was imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and providers who avoided liability caps

for.name: Rep. Christopher Cox
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House [S1][S3].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: The record shows the bill sent to the committee's Health Subcommittee on February 25, 2005, and no markup, hearing, or vote for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 136 of the bill's 141 cosponsors were Republicans, with only 5 Democrats signing on [S4].

industries.note: Damage caps and tighter filing deadlines would make payouts smaller and more predictable, cutting insurers' worst-case exposure. The savings would flow to insurers and policyholder doctors, with no requirement that patients see any of it.

The bill bars punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved drugs and devices and shields prescribing providers from product suits, insulating the industry from the punitive-damages verdicts that drive major product-safety litigation.

Providers would face capped damages, a higher bar for punitive awards, and shorter filing windows, reducing their malpractice exposure and insurance costs. The tradeoff is that patients injured by negligence would recover less.
The sliding-scale fee caps would directly cut contingency fees on malpractice cases, and the damage caps would shrink recoveries — the lawyers' fee base — especially in catastrophic-injury cases.

industries.industry: Health insurers and government benefit programs
industries.note: The bill would stop insurers and programs from placing liens on patients' awards or recovering subrogation claims, but it also lets defendants introduce evidence of collateral benefits in malpractice suits.
